lines: A system that keeps its data sorted on disk, in separate pieces, faces an awkward question every time someone asks for a key that simply isn't there: which of those pieces should it even bother opening?

One earlier design answered that almost for free, by keeping a small, cheap structure that can say 'definitely not here' most of the time, at a cost of only a handful of bits for every key it was built from.
That structure is occasionally wrong on purpose. The question for today is exactly how wrong it's allowed to be, and what it costs to make it far less wrong.
Here is the whole mechanism. Take a row of empty slots, and a handful of independent ways to pick a slot from any given key.
Storing a key means flipping on every one of the slots its own ways point to.
Asking about a key means checking those same slots. If even one of them is still off, the answer is a flat, certain no. If every one of them is on, the answer is only a maybe.
And notice what never happens here: a slot that's been switched on never gets switched back off by this structure on its own.
Suppose two completely different keys happen to point at the very same slot, and that slot is already switched on from the first one.
The second key comes along and tries to switch that same slot on too.
What actually happens to that slot?
answer: Nothing happens to it — it was already on, and it stays on.
This structure never tracks who flipped a slot or how many keys share it, only whether it's on or off, and that's precisely why a maybe can never be undone into a certain yes.

lines: Here's the derivation, and it only takes one line of reasoning. Every time a key is stored, each of its slots gets a chance to be switched on.
After a great many keys have been stored, the odds that one particular slot is still off settle into a clean, shrinking curve.

A wrong maybe needs every single one of a key's slots to already be on from something else — so the odds of that happening are that same shrinking curve, multiplied by itself once for every slot a key checks.
Build a real version of this and measure it at several different amounts of memory per key, and the actual wrong-answer rate lands right where that reasoning says it should, every time.
Given a fixed amount of memory per key, there turns out to be a best number of slots to check for each one.
Too few slots, and the same handful get reused too often. Too many, and each additional slot stops buying much improvement.
Right at that best number, something clean falls out: exactly half of every slot in the whole structure ends up switched on.
And the curve around that best number is remarkably flat — a slot more or fewer barely changes anything, which is exactly why real implementations feel free to round that number however's convenient.
Here's a number worth sitting with. Going from one wrong answer in a hundred down to one wrong answer in a million means getting it right ten thousand times more often.
Does reaching that requires something like ten thousand times the memory for every key stored?
answer: No — it takes only a small, fixed number of additional bits for every key, nowhere close to ten thousand times the memory.
Each additional bit per key multiplies the wrong-answer rate down by roughly the same constant factor every time, so reaching a much rarer rate costs addition in memory, never multiplication.

lines: Step back from this one structure entirely and ask a harder question: could any structure at all, built to never give a false no, do meaningfully better than this one does?

There's a clean counting argument that says no. Any such structure, representing a set this size at a wrong-answer rate this rare, needs at least a certain fixed number of bits per key — full stop, regardless of how it's built inside.

And the structure built from slots and independent probes doesn't fall far short of that floor. It sits within one fixed, unchanging multiple of the best anything could possibly do — and that multiple never grows, no matter how rare the target rate gets.
If checking several slots per key calls for several ways to pick a slot, here's the question worth asking before building anything.
Does each of those slot-picking rules need to be built and computed completely independently of the others, or could far fewer actually do the job?
answer: Far fewer — as few as two, combined arithmetically, can stand in for however many are needed.
Take two values computed independently and combine them with a small varying step, and the results land across just as many distinct slots as a whole collection of separately built rules would.

lines: Here's the trick made concrete. Compute two values from a key, then generate every slot a key needs by adding one of those values to a small, varying multiple of the other.

Build that version and a version using a whole collection of genuinely independent slot-picking rules, run both at the same amount of memory per key, and measure the wrong-answer rate each one actually produces.
They land on essentially the same number. Two combined values do the work that an entire collection of independent ones would have done, with no real loss.
Now for the one thing this structure flatly cannot do: take something back out.

Switching off one key's slots to 'remove' it switches off slots that other keys may depend on just as much — and suddenly a key that's still genuinely there gets a certain, wrong no. That's precisely the kind of mistake this structure promised could never happen.
This isn't a hand-picked worst case either — searching through a small version of the structure finds a real instance of exactly this failure without much effort at all.
An unchanging collection of keys, built once and never edited afterward, simply never runs into this, because nothing ever needs to be taken back out of it.
Recall the number from an earlier lesson: about ten bits of memory for every key, checked against a widely cited table, coming out to roughly one wrong answer in a hundred, using seven slots per key.
That number was never a separate fact to memorize. Plug that same amount of memory per key into today's one line of reasoning, and the exact same number falls straight out.
So here's where this one structure lands. It spends a little more than the fewest bits any structure possibly could, just to answer one yes-or-no question about one key.
And it pays for that savings in two ways: every yes is only ever a maybe, never a certainty, and the structure can neither take a key back out nor list what it's holding at all.
